metadata.title: Can older workers stay productive? The role of ICT skills and training

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Korean sample from the OECD PIAAC cross-sectional adult assessment (adults aged 16–65) and restricts the analytic sample to full-time workers working at least 30 hours per week, excluding self-employed individuals because wages are not reported. The paper does not report the use of PIAAC sampling weights or any replicate-weight variance estimation (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it instead focuses on regression specifications with robust standard errors. Because the analysis is not framed as a survey-weighted ILSA achievement model and no weight variable name is provided, the weighting strategy cannot be verified from the text. The key preprocessing steps are construction of a composite ICT skills measure (proficiency + workplace use), standardization of scores, and multiple imputation for missing ICT proficiency scores.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Uses the Korean sample from the PIAAC survey. Restricts to full-time workers aged 16–65 who worked at least 30 hours per week. Excludes self-employed individuals because wages are not reported. Constructs the wage outcome from hourly earnings (log hourly earnings). For ICT skills, combines (i) problem-solving in technology-rich environments proficiency and (ii) workplace ICT use index; ICT proficiency is missing for respondents who never used a computer, refused the computer-based assessment, or failed the ICT core/basic assessment, and these missing proficiency values are handled via multiple imputation.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 (Korea) adult assessment; outcome: log hourly earnings; subset: full-time workers (>=30h/week), ages 16–65
main_findings.target_variable: Wage (log hourly earnings) — effect of ICT skills and job training by age group
main_findings.performance_metrics: Table 2 (OLS Mincer-type regressions with robust SEs): ICT skills coefficient (Column 1) = 0.166 (SE 0.014); wage effect of ICT skills by age group: ICT skills x 50–65 = 0.029 (SE 0.037, not significant); job training x 50–65 = 0.154 (SE 0.062, significant at **); R-Square ranges 0.391–0.400; Observations 2620 (except Column 1 shows 2624). Additional analysis (Wage (log hourly earnings) — heterogeneous ICT skills returns for older workers by education and occupation): Table 3: ICT skills coefficient on reference young group = 0.153 (SE 0.025, significant at *); ICT skills x 50–65 x High Edu = 0.137 (SE 0.069, significant at **); ICT skills x 50–65 x Skill Occ = 0.129 (SE 0.044, significant at **); job training x 50–65 = 0.149 (SE 0.062, significant at **); R-Square 0.401–0.402; Observations 2620.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 (Korea) data for full-time workers (>=30h/week) aged 16–65, the study leveraged ICT skills composite index, job training participation, and controls including age, education, and literacy skills to model log hourly earnings, finding that ICT skills are positively associated with wages and that job training has a statistically significant larger wage effect for workers aged 50–65. This indicates that policies supporting ICT upskilling and especially job-related training for older workers may mitigate productivity decline associated with aging, though the estimates rely on observational identification and imputation rather than randomized causal effects.

data.outcome_summary: The paper uses the Korean sample from the OECD PIAAC adult assessment (2012) and restricts the analysis to full-time workers working at least 30 hours per week (N=2620), excluding self-employed respondents. The dependent variable is log hourly earnings, and the key ICT construct is a composite index combining standardized problem-solving in technology-rich environments proficiency with standardized workplace ICT use (equal weight 0.5). Missing ICT proficiency scores (25.9%) are handled via regression-based multiple imputation using literacy and numeracy as predictors, and literacy is also included in wage regressions as a proxy for unobserved ability. In Table 2, ICT skills show a positive wage association (coefficient 0.166 in Column 1), while job training has a significantly larger wage effect for ages 50–65 (interaction coefficient 0.154). In Table 3, the ICT skills returns for older workers are significantly higher when they are highly educated (ICT x 50–65 x High Edu = 0.137) or employed in skill-intensive occupations (ICT x 50–65 x Skill Occ = 0.129). Limitations include observational identification challenges and the fact that the analysis is econometric rather than ML predictive modeling.
